stem.en: The label on a cooking oil pack says one litre (910 g). One litre of water has a mass of about 1000 g. If this oil is mixed with water and left to stand, what happens?

text.en: Water goes on top, because water has more mass in each litre.
Oil goes on top, because one litre of oil has less mass than one litre of water. A separating funnel can then remove the water first.
Oil goes to the bottom, because 910 is a large mass for a pack of oil.
No layers form, because both are liquids that a kitchen uses every day.

explanation.en: Compare the same volume. One litre of oil is 910 g and one litre of water is about 1000 g, so the oil is less dense and it floats. The tempting slip is to think that more mass in a litre means going up: the denser liquid sinks. Cooking oil and water are immiscible, so two layers form, and the stopcock of a separating funnel releases the water first.

hints.en: Compare the mass of the same volume of each liquid.
Does the denser liquid float or sink?
